name: Amazon CloudFront
summary: AWS’s CDN: more than 750 edge locations that cache your S3 files and front your load balancers and APIs.
intro: You create a distribution, which gets a domain like `d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net`, and point it at one or more origins: an S3 bucket, a load balancer, API Gateway, or any HTTP server. Cache behaviours match URL path patterns such as `/api/*` or `/assets/*`, and each one picks an origin and its own caching rules. By default an object stays in an edge cache for 24 hours unless the origin’s headers say otherwise. On a miss, the edge location asks a larger regional edge cache before going to the origin, so the origin sees far fewer requests.

Two kinds of edge code run inside it. CloudFront Functions are tiny JavaScript functions (up to 10 KB) that run in under a millisecond on every request, good for redirects, header changes and cache-key cleanup. Lambda@Edge runs Node.js or Python for up to 30 seconds and can call the network. What sets CloudFront apart is how it fits into AWS: fetching cacheable content from AWS origins such as S3, ALB or API Gateway costs nothing for data transfer, and you pay only for bytes and requests going out to viewers. AWS also offers flat-rate plans, from free to $1,000 a month, that bundle the CDN with WAF, DNS and no overage charges.
strengths: Data transfer of cacheable content from AWS origins such as S3, ALB and API Gateway to CloudFront is free
Always-free tier of 1 TB out, 10 million requests and 2 million CloudFront Functions invocations a month
Origin access control lets you keep an S3 bucket private and serve it only through the distribution
Per-path cache behaviours let one domain serve static files from S3 and dynamic requests from a load balancer
limits: ACM certificates for a distribution must be issued in `us-east-1`, whatever region the rest of your stack is in
Only the first 1,000 invalidation paths a month are free; use versioned file names instead of purging
Default ceilings of 150 Gbps and 250,000 requests per second per distribution need a quota request to raise
Lambda@Edge on viewer events gets only 128 MB of memory and can return at most 40 KB

story: When S3 launched in 2006, customers soon asked AWS for a way to secure and speed up delivery of their files to users around the world. The established CDNs, such as Akamai and Limelight, sold their service on long-term contracts, which suited big media companies better than small ones.

AWS launched Amazon CloudFront in beta on 18 November 2008 with 14 edge locations: eight in the US, four in Europe and two in Asia. It worked the AWS way, with no contract and a pay-as-you-go price starting at $0.17 per GB in the US and Europe. At first every origin had to be an S3 bucket and there was no HTTPS.

CloudFront then grew in steps. Custom origins in 2010 let it front any web server, regional edge caches in 2016 added a middle tier to protect origins, and Lambda@Edge, previewed the same year, began a line of edge code that led to CloudFront Functions in 2021. Today it has more than 750 edge locations.

choices.choice: Pay as you go, no contracts
choices.why: Traditional CDNs locked customers into long-term deals. Metered, self-service pricing matched the rest of AWS and opened CDNs to small companies.

choices.choice: Start with S3 as the only origin
choices.why: The demand came from S3 users, so the first version only cached objects from S3 buckets. Support for any HTTP server followed two years later.

choices.choice: A regional cache tier between edge and origin
choices.why: With hundreds of edge locations, each miss going straight to the origin multiplied its load. Larger regional edge caches, added in 2016, catch many of those misses first.

choices.choice: Run code at the edge in two sizes
choices.why: Lambda@Edge handles heavier logic with network access, while CloudFront Functions (2021) run tiny JavaScript on every request in under a millisecond, cheap enough for header rewrites and redirects.

timeline.text: CloudFront launches in beta on 18 November with 14 edge locations
Custom origins let it serve from any HTTP server, not just S3
Regional edge caches added; Lambda@Edge previewed (GA in July 2017)
CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript on every request
HTTP/3 support; origin access control succeeds the older origin access identity
Flat-rate plans from $0 to $1,000 a month bundle CDN, WAF and DNS
